questions.q: On Montalcino's slopes, which soil does the Court place at the higher elevations, above the clay and marine sediments lower down?
questions.exp: The Court's cell splits Montalcino by height: clay and marine sediments on the lower slopes and galestro, the flaky, friable marl also found in the Chianti hills, higher up, where it drains freely and is prized for Sangiovese.

questions.q: Beyond moderate colour and tart acidity that outweighs the tannin, which character does the Court say is common in Sangiovese based wines?
questions.exp: The Court's style cell reads Sangiovese as moderate in colour with tart acidity that outweighs its tannin, and notes that volatile acidity, a lift of vinegar or nail varnish, is common in these wines; a touch can add lift, too much is a fault.

questions.q: What share of a Brunello di Montalcino must come from Sangiovese?
questions.exp: Brunello di Montalcino is 100 per cent Sangiovese, the local selection long called Brunello, as the Court prints it, where Chianti Classico needs at least 80 per cent and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano at least 70.

questions.q: Which DOC takes the younger, earlier released Sangiovese of the Vino Nobile zone?
questions.exp: Rosso di Montepulciano DOC sits beneath Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG as the zone's younger wine, the pair the Court lists; Rosso di Montalcino plays the same part beneath Brunello, and Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is named for a grape, not the Tuscan town.

questions.q: Le Pergole Torte, among the top wines the Court names, is made entirely from which grape?
questions.exp: Le Pergole Torte, from the Montevertine estate at Radda in Chianti, has been pure Sangiovese since 1977 and is sold as IGT by choice; the Court prints it as La Pergole Torte, beside Bordeaux variety wines such as Masseto (Merlot) and Solaia.

questions.q: Beyond its two years in wood, how many months must a standard Brunello di Montalcino rest in bottle before release?
questions.exp: Brunello must spend at least two years in oak, large Slavonian casks or small barriques as the Court says, and at least four months in bottle, and may be released only from 1 January of the fifth year after the harvest; the Riserva needs six months in bottle and the sixth year.
